lines.text: In twenty twenty one, more than a million deaths worldwide were caused directly by bacteria that antibiotics could no longer kill.

visual.file: File:Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus Aureus (MRSA) Bacteria colorized scanning electron micrograph - 11.jpg

lines.text: Resistant infections were linked to about four point seven million deaths that year.
The medicines that changed modern medicine are slowly losing their power.
This is the story of how it happened, and what still works.

visual.file: File:Medical laboratory, Where science, medicine converge 140417-F-FM358-007.jpg

lines.text: When antibiotics stop working.

visual.bg: File:Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus Aureus (MRSA) Bacteria colorized scanning electron micrograph - 11.jpg

lines.text: Chapter one. The mould that changed medicine.
In nineteen twenty eight, Alexander Fleming noticed something strange on a culture plate.
A mould had landed on it, and the bacteria around it had died.
That mould gave us penicillin, the first antibiotic to change medicine.
Before antibiotics, a simple infection could be a death sentence. Afterwards, medicine could take risks it never could before.
Today, joint replacements, organ transplants and cancer therapy all depend on being able to treat infections.
Resistance raises the risk of complications from procedures like surgery.

visual.file: File:Medical laboratory, Where science, medicine converge 140417-F-FM358-007.jpg

lines.text: Chapter two. How bacteria fight back.
Resistance happens when germs develop the ability to defeat the drugs designed to kill them.
Every time an antibiotic is used, it puts pressure on bacteria to adapt.
Picture billions of bacteria in an infection. A few carry a random genetic change that helps them survive the drug.
The antibiotic kills the rest. The survivors now have room to multiply.
lines.ost: Survival of the fittest|The resistant ones multiply

lines.text: That's evolution, happening in days instead of millions of years.
They have four main tricks.
Some make enzymes that break the antibiotic down.
Some pump it straight back out, or change the target so the drug no longer fits.
And some close the doors it uses to get in.
Worse, bacteria can share resistance with other bacteria that have never even seen the drug.
They pass it on through mobile pieces of DNA, which is why resistance can spread so fast.
Medical students, this is classic exam material. Enzymes, efflux pumps, target changes and reduced entry.
Chapter three. The scale of the problem.
In twenty twenty three, about one in six lab-confirmed bacterial infections worldwide were resistant to antibiotics.
Between twenty eighteen and twenty twenty three, resistance rose in over forty percent of the drug and bug pairs WHO tracks.

visual.file: File:Medical laboratory, Where science, medicine converge 140417-F-FM358-007.jpg

lines.text: Two gut bacteria keep topping these lists: E. coli and Klebsiella.
lines.ost: The leaders|E. coli and K. pneumoniae

lines.text: Globally, more than forty percent of E. coli and over fifty five percent of Klebsiella resist the first-choice antibiotics for these infections.
Even powerful drugs like carbapenems are losing effectiveness against Klebsiella and Acinetobacter.
And M R S A, a resistant staph, caused over a hundred thousand deaths in a single year on its own.

visual.file: File:Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus Aureus (MRSA) Bacteria colorized scanning electron micrograph - 11.jpg

lines.text: Older people are hit hardest. Since nineteen ninety, resistance deaths in people over seventy have risen by more than eighty percent.

visual.label: AMR DEATHS, AGE 70+, 1990-2021
visual.sub: While deaths in under-5s more than halved

lines.text: Chapter four. Why it matters for South Asia.
WHO estimates resistance is highest in its South-East Asia and Eastern Mediterranean regions, where one in three reported infections were resistant.
lines.ost: WHO South-East Asia|1 in 3 infections resistant

lines.text: And forecasts in The Lancet put South Asia among the regions with the highest death rates from resistance by twenty fifty.
lines.ost: Forecast to 2050|South Asia among the hardest hit

lines.text: Resistant germs spread in hospitals, in the community, through food and the environment, and between people and animals.
Chapter five. What actually works.

visual.title: What actually works
visual.sub: For doctors, students and everyone else

lines.text: First, use antibiotics only when they're needed. Ask your doctor whether you really need one.
Colds are viral, and trials show antibiotics don't help them.
Antibiotics also have side effects. In cold trials, adults given antibiotics had more of them than those on placebo.
Second, prevent infections. Clean hands are one of the best ways to stop germs spreading.
Vaccines prevent infections too, including resistant ones.
For clinicians: prescribe only when the benefits outweigh the risks, and pick the right drug.
So, to recap. Resistance is caused by germs adapting under antibiotic pressure, and it spreads between bacteria, people and animals.
It already causes over a million deaths a year, and it's highest in regions like ours.
lines.ost: Recap|Over a million deaths a year

lines.text: Antimicrobial resistance is a major global health threat. But it isn't a lost battle.
lines.ost: A major threat|Not a lost battle

visual.file: File:Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus Aureus (MRSA) Bacteria colorized scanning electron micrograph - 11.jpg

lines.text: Every antibiotic we don't need to use keeps the ones we have working longer.

titles: When Antibiotics Stop Working: The Superbug Crisis Explained
How Bacteria Beat Antibiotics, and What Still Works
meta.summary: Drug-resistant bacteria directly caused 1.14 million deaths in 2021 and were linked to about 4.7 million. This deep dive covers how penicillin changed medicine, the four ways bacteria resist antibiotics, what WHO's 2025 surveillance found (1 in 6 infections resistant worldwide, 1 in 3 in WHO's South-East Asia region), and what actually works: using antibiotics only when needed, preventing infections, vaccines and stewardship.

meta.verdict: AMR directly caused 1.14 million deaths in 2021; resistance is rising; prudent use, prevention and vaccines work.
